title: Did Christianity Copy Pagan Myths?
excerpt: The claim that the story of Jesus was copied from Horus, Mithras and other pagan gods is older than the internet, and it can be checked against the ancient sources it seldom cites.
body:
In 2007 a filmmaker named Peter Joseph released a documentary called *Zeitgeist*, and its first section made an argument that has followed the church around the internet ever since. Long before Jesus, the film said, the Egyptian god Horus was born of a virgin on December 25. A star in the east announced him, and three kings came to find him. He taught at twelve, was baptized at thirty, gathered twelve disciples and worked miracles. Then he was crucified, lay dead three days, and rose. The film said much the same of Attis, Krishna, Dionysus and Mithras. Jesus, it concluded, is an old story about the sun with new names.

The idea is older than the film. In 1875 an American freethinker named Kersey Graves published *The World's Sixteen Crucified Saviors*, a catalogue of gods said to have died for humanity before Jesus did. Graves gave his readers almost nothing they could check against an ancient text. Even Richard Carrier, a historian who argues that Jesus probably never existed, has called the book unreliable. The list survived anyway. It has passed from book to book for a century and a half.

Most people meet it in a form that's hard to answer on the spot, a meme or a friend who has just watched the video. A Christian who was never told the question existed can be badly shaken. A skeptic may think it settles the matter. If the story of Jesus was assembled from older myths, then believing it is like believing in Horus, and nobody believes in Horus anymore. The way to answer it is to read what the old sources actually say.

## What Is True in the Claim

Christianity was born in a world crowded with gods. When Paul walked through Athens, Luke says, the city was full of idols. Paul began his speech on the Areopagus by granting what he had seen: "Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious" (Acts 17:22). Temples of Isis stood in port cities around the Mediterranean. Mystery cults offered initiation and the hope of a better lot after death. A new faith was bound to be compared with all of it.

The first comparisons weren't made by modern skeptics. Late in the second century a pagan philosopher named Celsus wrote an attack on the Christians. His Jewish spokesman asks why Jesus' rising should be treated differently from the tales the Greeks told, and he runs through a list that includes Orpheus, Heracles, Theseus, Pythagoras, and an Egyptian king said to have played dice with Demeter in the underworld. Celsus wanted to know whether the Christians imagined "the statements of others not only to be myths, but to have the appearance of such," while their own story was credible. We have his words because Origen quoted them in order to answer them.

Christians noticed the likeness too. Around the middle of the second century Justin, a Christian philosopher teaching in Rome, wrote an appeal to the emperor on the church's behalf. When Christians say that Jesus "was crucified and died, and rose again, and ascended into heaven," Justin told him, "we propound nothing different from what you believe regarding those whom you esteem sons of Jupiter." He named several, among them Bacchus "after he had been torn limb from limb." He also said that in the mysteries of Mithras bread and a cup of water were set out at initiations, in imitation of the Lord's Supper.

About half a century later Tertullian of Carthage wrote that, "if my memory still serves me," Mithras marked his soldiers on the forehead, offered bread, and "introduces an image of a resurrection." Christians wrote down some of these resemblances before their critics did.

Some of the borrowing ran the way the critics say. The New Testament gives no date for Jesus' birth. The first clear evidence for December 25 is a Roman calendar compiled in 354, which lists the birth of Christ in Bethlehem on that day and also marks it as the birthday of the Unconquered, a title of the sun. Historians still argue about the connection. Some think the church chose the date to answer a festival of the sun. Others point to an old Christian reckoning, passed on by Augustine, that Jesus was conceived on March 25, which puts his birth nine months later. Either way, it was the church that chose the date.

The church also adapted on purpose. In 601 Pope Gregory the Great wrote to the abbot Mellitus, who was on his way to the mission in England, that the temples of idols there "should not be destroyed, but that the idols themselves that are in them should be." The buildings were to be sprinkled with holy water and turned into churches, and the old feasts made into feasts for the martyrs. "It is undoubtedly impossible to cut away everything at once from hard hearts," Gregory explained. More than a century later Bede recorded that the month in which the English kept Easter had been named for a goddess called Eostre. The Christmas tree and the yule log came out of the folk customs of Europe as well. None of it came from the Bible.

So on these points the critics are right. The first Christians lived among pagans, and the church later took over some of its neighbors' customs. But *Zeitgeist* isn't arguing about the date of Christmas. It claims that the center of the faith, a man crucified and raised on the third day, was taken from older myths. A claim like that needs different evidence, and it has to be tested against what the ancient sources say about Horus, Mithras and the rest.

## Where the Lists Came From

The modern form of the argument has a history of its own. In 1890 the Scottish scholar James George Frazer published the first edition of *The Golden Bough*, a vast comparison of myth and ritual. There and in the larger editions that followed, he gathered Adonis, Attis and Osiris into a family of gods who died and rose with the crops. The god went down with the harvest and came back with the spring. It wasn't far from Frazer's pages to the idea that Easter belonged in the same family. For a generation the idea had real standing in the universities. German scholars of what came to be called the History of Religions School argued that Paul's talk of being "buried therefore with him by baptism into death" (Romans 6:4) owed something to the mystery cults.

Over the next century specialists went back to the ancient texts one god at a time, and Frazer's family came apart. The popular lists never caught up. What circulates online is mostly the older version, with Graves's confidence and no more sources than he gave.

## Testing the Claims Against the Sources

Start with Horus, since he heads the list. The fullest ancient telling of his family's story comes from Plutarch, a Greek writer and priest at Delphi, who wrote it down early in the second century. In it Typhon, the Greek name for the god Seth, tricks his brother Osiris into lying down in a chest, and the plotters shut him in. Isis, Osiris's sister and wife, finds the chest at Byblos. Typhon later finds the body while hunting by moonlight and tears it into fourteen pieces, and Isis gathers them from the marshes. Horus is already a child by then. A second son, Harpocrates, is conceived when "Osiris consorted with Isis after his death."

There is no virgin in Plutarch's story, no star in the east, no baptism at thirty, no band of twelve, no cross and no third day. Osiris doesn't walk out of a tomb either. The priests, Plutarch says, teach that "this god Osiris is the ruler and king of the dead," so his return is a reign in the underworld, which is a very different thing from a body leaving a grave.

Plutarch does give the critics something. Some people in his day tied the story to the farming year, saying that Osiris "is being buried at the time when the grain is sown" and "comes to life and reappears when plants begin to sprout," and that Harpocrates was born "about the time of the winter solstice." So the seasonal reading is ancient, and a solstice birth does appear in a pagan source. Plutarch, a devout pagan, thought these interpreters "numerous and tiresome." Even in their reading, though, it's a story about what happens every year.

Mithras is harder to test, because his followers left almost no writing behind. The god Mithra is very old in Persia. Plutarch says the Cilician pirates whom Pompey fought in the 60s before Christ practiced "certain secret rites, among which those of Mithras continue to the present time." But the Roman mysteries of Mithras are known mostly from the shrines their members built from the late first century on, small cave-like halls decorated with the scene of Mithras killing a bull. The poet Statius, writing around AD 90, pictured him twisting the horns beneath the rocks of a Persian cave.

Christian writers who watched the cult recorded what struck them. Justin says its members claimed Mithras was "begotten of a rock" and initiated their converts in a cave. Both he and Tertullian mention bread in the cult's rites, and Tertullian adds a mark on the forehead. Those are real resemblances, mostly in ritual. But no surviving source tells a story of Mithras dying. In the monuments he is the one who kills, and a god whose story has no death in it can't be the pattern for a man who was crucified and raised.

Dionysus is a better candidate. Justin himself repeats the story that Bacchus was torn to pieces and "ascended into heaven." He was also the god of wine. Pausanias, a Greek traveler of the second century, describes a festival at Elis where priests sealed three empty pots in a building overnight and found them full of wine in the morning. Pausanias admits he wasn't there to see it. Some scholars think John's story of the wine at Cana was told with Dionysus in mind. Others hear in it the prophets, who promised that "the mountains shall drip sweet wine" (Amos 9:13).

His birth doesn't fit the list at all. Euripides' *Bacchae*, staged at the end of the fifth century before Christ, opens with Dionysus naming his parents: Zeus and Semele, a mortal princess of Thebes. Zeus's lightning killed her as she gave birth. Her sisters' slander in the play is that she slept with a mortal man and blamed Zeus. Nobody in the story imagines a virgin. Justin did compare the virgin birth with the Greek story of Perseus, the son of Danae, so the comparison is an old one. But Justin also pointed out that the poets had Jupiter forcing himself on "those many women whom he had violated." Whatever Luke means by the angel's word to Mary, he doesn't mean that.

The clearest pagan rising that survives belongs to Adonis. A second-century treatise on the Syrian goddess, traditionally credited to Lucian, describes the rites at Byblos. Each year the people mourn the young man killed by a boar. They make offerings to him as to the dead, and the next day they declare that he is alive. That is a real parallel. But it was written down about a century after Paul's letters, and what it describes is a festival held every year.

## What the Specialists Concluded

The scholar who did most to take Frazer's scheme apart was Jonathan Z. Smith, a historian of religion at the University of Chicago whose work had nothing to do with defending Christianity. In a 1987 encyclopedia article on dying and rising gods, Smith argued that the category was largely a misnomer. It rested, he said, on imaginative reconstruction and on texts that were very late or very unclear. Some of Frazer's gods die and don't come back to the living, like Osiris. Others disappear for a while and return without having died. And much of the evidence for a celebrated rising, like the one at Byblos, comes from writers who lived after Christianity had begun.

Not everyone agreed, and a Christian who cites Smith as if the matter were closed is claiming more than the field does. Tryggve Mettinger, a Swedish Old Testament scholar, later argued that some gods of the ancient Near East, Dumuzi and Baal among them, really were understood to die and return with the seasons. He thought Smith had gone too far. He also wrote that, as far as he was aware, there was no evidence, on the face of it, that the Christian proclamation of Jesus' death and resurrection had been built from those myths.

Bart Ehrman came at the question from outside the faith. He is an agnostic, and in *Did Jesus Exist?* he took up the pagan parallels. Many writers who repeat lists like Graves's, he has written, have taken them on without checking, and the ancient evidence for gods who died and rose again is thin. The resemblances that are real don't show that Jesus was invented. In his reading the belief that God had raised Jesus grew out of Jewish hope for the end of the age. Ehrman doesn't believe Jesus rose. He just doesn't think copying explains why his followers said he did. Whether Jesus existed is its own question, taken up in [Was Jesus Real?](/writing/the-historical-jesus)

## Why Easter Does Not Fit the Pattern

A seasonal myth is about what always happens: the god goes into the ground with the grain and comes back when it sprouts, this year and next year and every year. Nobody asks which year Osiris died, because the question makes no sense.

The Christian story is set in a particular year. Luke dates the beginning of John the Baptist's preaching the way a historian dates a reign: "In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea" (Luke 3:1). Tacitus, a Roman historian who despised the Christians, wrote that Christus "suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus." The church even wrote him into its creed: Jesus "suffered under Pontius Pilate." A myth about the seasons has no use for a provincial governor.

And it happened once. "We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him" (Romans 6:9). A god of the harvest has to die again next autumn, or his story stops working. The church keeps Easter every year, as Israel keeps Passover, but what it remembers happened one time.

What Paul meant by resurrection came from the Jews. Many Jews of Jesus' day hoped for the resurrection of the dead, and they meant it bodily. "Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise," Isaiah had promised (Isaiah 26:19). Second Maccabees, written in the generations before Jesus, tells of seven brothers tortured to death under the Syrian king Antiochus IV for keeping the law of Moses. One of them holds out his hands to the torturers and says he hopes to receive them back from God. That hope was for all the righteous together, when God brought this age to its end.

The first people to say that God had raised Jesus were Jews, and they said it in those terms. Paul handed on to the Corinthians what he had received: that Christ "was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:4). Then he listed the people Jesus appeared to, naming some and counting others, among them "more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive" (1 Corinthians 15:6). The evidence for those appearances is weighed in [Did the Resurrection Actually Happen?](/writing/did-the-resurrection-happen)

The pagans who first heard it didn't hear something familiar. Celsus thought the Christian story a myth like the others, and his complaint shows that the Christians kept insisting it wasn't. The death itself was nothing like a hero's. Heracles climbed onto his own pyre, and the poets said he rose from it to the gods. Jesus was executed by the state the way Rome executed slaves and rebels, and Paul, quoting the law of Moses, said of such a death, "Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree" (Galatians 3:13). Nobody borrowing from the heroes would have chosen that.

## Where Christians Have Overstated Their Case

Christians haven't always answered this well, and some of our answers have made things worse. Justin thought demons had heard the prophets and invented the sons of Jupiter ahead of time, so that the story of Christ would sound like "mere marvellous tales, like the things which were said by the poets." Tertullian said the devil imitates the sacraments. That answer can account for any resemblance at all, and nothing could ever test it. It also concedes the point the critics most want, that the stories are alike in substance. A Christian who reaches for something like it today hasn't looked at the sources any more closely than the person who made the list.

The opposite reflex is just as common, and it says there are no real parallels at all. There are. Tertullian knew that initiates of Isis and Mithras were washed in water and that the followers of Mithras offered bread. The people of Byblos said Adonis lived again. Deny all of it to a well-read skeptic, and you'll lose him on the first point he checks.

Some say the Mithras cult came after Christianity, so the copying must have run the other way. That's too quick. Plutarch places rites of Mithras among pirates decades before Jesus was born, and the Roman mysteries grew up in the same centuries as the church. Influence in either direction is hard to prove. The sources support a narrower claim: no ancient text gives Mithras a death, so there was no resurrection to borrow.

Others say first-century Jews were sealed off from Greek ideas. Martin Hengel, a German New Testament scholar, showed in the 1960s how far Greek language and culture had spread through the Jewish homeland in the centuries before Jesus. Yet many Jews who lived among Greeks still went to their deaths rather than sacrifice to a Greek god. Paul praised converts who "turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God" (1 Thessalonians 1:9). A movement that counted conversion that way was an unlikely place to borrow a rising god from the cults it had told people to leave.

And some of the ammunition came from my own side of the Reformation. Alexander Hislop, a Scottish minister, first published *The Two Babylons* in 1853. It argued that the Roman Catholic Church was the religion of ancient Babylon in Christian dress. Hislop claimed, among much else, that Easter was really the goddess Astarte, whom the Assyrians called Ishtar. The book is still in print, and every spring its Easter claim goes around social media again, aimed now at every Christian. There is no connection between the English word Easter and the name Ishtar. The link was popularized by a Protestant attack on Rome.

Smith argued in a later book that the scholarly comparison of early Christianity with the pagan cults also grew up inside Protestant polemics, as a way of showing that Catholic sacraments were paganism that had crept into a pure early church. The skeptic's version needed only one more step. If the Mass came from the mysteries, why not the resurrection?

Ralph Woodrow, an evangelical writer, popularized Hislop in the 1960s in a book called *Babylon Mystery Religion*. Years later he went back to Hislop's sources, found they didn't hold up, and withdrew his own book. Then he wrote another explaining why. That is rarer than it should be. Most of us are slow to check a claim that helps our side. If *Zeitgeist* makes us angry, we might ask how many unchecked claims we have passed along because they made the faith look good. The film and Hislop's book were built the same way, out of resemblances and an audience that wouldn't look up the sources.

## What the Old Stories Tell Us

Paul didn't treat the religions of Athens as nonsense. He told the Athenians he had found an altar inscribed "To the unknown god" (Acts 17:23), and he quoted their own poets to them. C.S. Lewis, who came to Christian faith partly through conversations with friends about these very myths, thought the resemblances were what you would expect if the human imagination had been reaching for something real. He called the story of Christ a true myth, one that works on us the way the others do, except that it happened. Lewis took more of Frazer for granted than the specialists now would. But he was right that all those stories of dying and returning gods show how badly people have wanted death undone.

Then Paul came to the resurrection, and that is where some of them laughed (Acts 17:32). They understood him well enough. He wasn't offering one more story about the turning of the year. He was telling them that God "has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead" (Acts 17:31).

That is a claim about a particular man and a particular tomb outside Jerusalem, and it has to be weighed like any other claim about the past. A list of gods can't settle it.

Do we hold the resurrection the way Paul did, as something that happened and has to be reckoned with? Or has it become, for us too, a lovely story about spring that nobody needs to check?

The longing in all those old myths wasn't foolish.

It was answered, once, by a man who will never die again.

*"For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty."* (2 Peter 1:16)

*"See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have."* (Luke 24:39)

*"And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain."* (1 Corinthians 15:14)
